analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators fine employer health plans that shortchange mental health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill has one cosponsor and has sat untouched in the House Education and Workforce Committee since the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act of 2008 already requires most health plans to cover mental health and substance use treatment no less generously than physical care, but federal regulators rarely penalize plans that violate it, partly because the penalties on the books are narrow. This bill writes civil monetary penalties for parity violations into the pension-law enforcement section, extends the fines to plan service providers and administrators as well as sponsors, clears the way for the Labor Department to enforce the rules directly, and gives the regulators $30 million a year for five years to do the work.
analysis.who_benefits: People with mental health or substance use conditions who are covered by employer-based health plans. Stronger fines and dedicated funding give the Labor Department a real stick to force plans to cover therapy, medication, detox, and rehab at parity with medical and surgical care, instead of quietly restricting them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in employer plans needing mental health care

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds civil monetary penalties for failing to meet the mental health parity requirements of the 2008 Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act, applying to group health plans and the insurers offering coverage under them starting a year after enactment.

It extends the penalty from plan sponsors alone to plan sponsors, service providers, and plan administrators, so the companies that administer claims and manage utilization review can be fined directly.

It removes a statutory obstacle so the Labor Secretary can enforce section 712 (parity in mental health and substance use disorder benefits), turning parity from a rule plans could mostly ignore into an enforceable one.
It appropriates $30,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2031 to the Employee Benefits Security Administration to enforce parity and the related genetic-information rules.

analysis.who_pays: Employer health plan sponsors and the insurers and third-party administrators behind them, who would face federal fines for parity violations and the cost of coming into compliance, costs that can partly show up in premiums. Taxpayers fund the $30 million a year.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health plans, their administrators, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The compliance and penalty costs fall on employers and plan administrators, and those costs are commonly passed into premiums, so some workers could see modestly higher health insurance costs.
The bill is narrow: the new penalties attach only to employer group health plans under the pension statute, not to coverage bought on the individual market, leaving part of the problem unaddressed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of people whose mental health claims are denied or limited more strictly than physical claims, enforceable fines and funded enforcement could change real access to care. The offsetting costs are real but modest relative to the scale of parity noncompliance, and they fall mostly on the plans whose practices the fines are meant to change. The bill's narrow reach is a fair criticism, not a fatal one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced at the end of June 2026 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has not taken it up, so it has never had a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Kean (R-NJ) introduced the bill on June 30, 2026, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
No further action has been listed since the referral — no hearing, markup, or vote.
The bill has a single cosponsor, a House Republican.

The bill's substance is a penalty and enforcement package: civil monetary fines for parity violations, liability extended to service providers and administrators, Secretary of Labor enforcement authority, and $30 million a year of appropriations for fiscal years 2027 through 2031.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health plans and their administrators are better off so far; with no movement on the bill, they continue to face no federal civil fines for parity violations.

for.name: Rep. Thomas H. Kean (R-NJ)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so the partisan shape is unrecorded; the sponsor and its only cosponsor are Republicans, and the Republican-led committee it went to has not acted.

industries.industry: Employer health plan sponsors, insurers, and third-party administrators
industries.note: These companies currently face essentially no civil fines when they restrict mental health and substance use benefits more than medical ones; the bill would make them finable and responsible for compliance costs. Their financial interest in avoiding fines runs against the interest of patients whose care gets restricted.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced this late in a session, with a single cosponsor and no committee action since referral, almost always die without a vote when the session ends in early January 2027. Unless the committee schedules it or it is attached to a larger bill, it will expire.
